theme: The visitors; Abraham intercedes; Sodom destroyed
readingInstruction: Read Genesis 18:1-19:38. These two chapters tell the linked stories of God’s visit to Abraham and the destruction of Sodom and Gomorrah. They belong together, the same God who promises blessing also brings judgment. Pay attention to Abraham’s bold intercession, Lot’s compromised life, and the contrasting endings of the two families.
settingTheScene: Abraham has been circumcised. The covenant has been renewed. Now three visitors arrive at Abraham’s tent in the heat of the day. One of them is the LORD himself. The visit will accomplish two things: confirm the imminent birth of Isaac, and reveal the coming judgment on Sodom. Today’s reading shows the close relationship between promise and judgment in the life of God’s people. The same God who blesses also judges. And in the middle of it all, Lot, Abraham’s compromised nephew, is rescued from the burning cities, barely.
observation: Abraham shows extravagant hospitality to the three visitors, washing their feet, preparing a feast, standing while they eat.
The LORD promises that Sarah will have a son “about this time next year.” Sarah laughs from inside the tent.
Sarah’s laughter is rebuked but not punished. God hears her, even when she denies laughing.
Verses 17-19 are striking: God deliberates whether to hide his plan from Abraham, then decides to reveal it.
Abraham’s intercession for Sodom (verses 22-33) moves in stages: 50, 45, 40, 30, 20, 10. Each request is bolder, but each is granted.
God’s openness to Abraham’s prayer is remarkable. The patriarch genuinely shapes the conversation.
Genesis 19 opens with Lot sitting in the gate of Sodom, a place of civic leadership. He has become a Sodomite in residence.
The men of Sodom demand to abuse the visitors. Lot offers his daughters instead, a horrifying response that shows how compromised he has become.
The angels strike the men with blindness and pull Lot back into the house. Even in his failure, God’s grace pursues him.
Lot’s wife looks back and becomes a pillar of salt. Lot’s daughters get him drunk and conceive, Moab and Ammon, future enemies of Israel.
interpretation:
Genesis 18 and 19 are one of the most stark contrasts in the Old Testament. The two chapters happen at the same time but in different places. In one, the LORD eats a meal with Abraham, promises a son, and listens to bold intercession. In the other, fire falls from heaven and ancient cities are destroyed. The same God acts in both. The difference is not in God; it is in the relationship those two households have with him.

The visit to Abraham is extraordinary. Three strangers arrive at his tent, and Abraham extravagantly serves them. Only as the meal unfolds does it become clear that one of them is the LORD himself, perhaps a pre-incarnate appearance of Christ, accompanied by two angels. The same LORD who promised Abraham a son is now sitting under his tree, eating his food, and confirming the timeline.

But the visit is also for another purpose. The LORD says, “Shall I hide from Abraham what I am about to do?” And he reveals the coming judgment on Sodom. This is what it means to be a friend of God, and Abraham is called the friend of God multiple times in Scripture. Friends are told things. Servants are given orders. Friends are admitted into the deliberations of their friend’s heart. Abraham is being told the future not so he can run for cover but so he can intercede.

And intercede he does. The negotiation between Abraham and God is one of the most remarkable passages in the Bible. Abraham works his way down, what if there are 50 righteous? 45? 40? 30? 20? 10? Each time, God agrees. Each time, Abraham draws nearer. This is not Abraham manipulating God. This is God inviting Abraham into a conversation about justice. The patriarch is being trained to think and feel as God does, caring about the righteous, longing for mercy, willing to plead for cities he does not even live in.

Then the scene shifts. Genesis 19 opens with Lot. He has come a long way from when he and Abram first separated. Lot is now sitting in the gate of Sodom, the place where civic leaders gather. He has become a man of standing in a wicked city. His compromise is total. When the angels arrive, the men of Sodom surround the house demanding to abuse them. Lot’s response is horrifying: he offers his own daughters to be raped instead. This is what years of living in Sodom have done to him. His moral center has so eroded that he is willing to sacrifice his daughters to maintain the cultural code of hospitality.

The angels rescue Lot anyway. They strike the attackers with blindness, drag Lot back into the house, and the next morning practically force him out of the city. “The LORD being merciful to him.” Lot is saved not because of his faithfulness but because of God’s mercy and Abraham’s prayer. This is one of the clearest pictures in the Old Testament of grace operating despite human failure.

The endings of the two stories are painfully different. Abraham’s tent ends in joy, laughter, food, promise, intercession. Lot’s home ends in flame, salt, drunkenness, and incest. The two daughters, having lost everything, get their father drunk and conceive children. The two children, Moab and Ammon, will become nations that war against Israel for centuries. Lot’s compromise produces a legacy of enemies. Abraham’s faithfulness produces a legacy of promise.

The lesson is clear and sobering. Where you choose to live matters. The company you keep matters. The cities of Sodom looked attractive to Lot when he first chose them; they cost him everything in the end. Abraham, who chose the harder hill country, was the one with whom the LORD shared his meals and his plans.
connection: The Abrahamic Covenant included the promise that God would “curse those who dishonor” Abraham. Today we see the inverse: God reveals his plans to Abraham as his friend, and rescues Abraham’s compromised nephew because of him. The intercession Abraham offers prefigures Christ’s intercession for his people, bold, persistent, asking for mercy on the basis of God’s character. And the destruction of Sodom prefigures the final judgment, which Jesus himself will compare to the days of Lot (Luke 17:28-32).
application:
Two warnings and one comfort.

First warning: be careful where you settle. Lot did not become wicked overnight. He drifted, decision by decision, into a city that ultimately consumed him. The places you choose to live, the people you choose to befriend, the environments you choose to immerse yourself in, these shape you over time. Do not assume you will be unaffected.

Second warning: take Christ’s words seriously. Jesus said, “Remember Lot’s wife” (Luke 17:32). She turned back. She had been told not to. And her brief, longing look backward froze her in place forever. Do not look back at what God is rescuing you out of. Move forward.

The comfort: Abraham interceded for Sodom, and Lot was rescued. Christ intercedes for his people, and we are rescued. If you know someone today who is compromised, who is sitting in the gate of Sodom, who is drifting away from God, pray for them. Stand before God on their behalf. Abraham’s intercession was not wasted, and yours will not be either.
prayerPrompts: Ask God to make you a friend he can trust with his purposes.
Pray for someone you love who is drifting toward compromise, in the way Abraham pleaded for Lot.
Confess any drift of your own, and ask him to turn you.
